    the next regression rather than on the debt already there.

    reliability_rating is D and sqale_rating is A; neither is in the gate. A
    rating condition that the project already fails would be red from the day
    it is switched on, and a gate that is red on arrival is one somebody turns

    A ratchet, so every threshold sits AT the current value: the gate fires on
    the next regression, not on the existing debt. Tighten deliberately, as
    debt is paid down.

    reliability_rating is E and sqale_rating is A. Neither is in the gate:
    E cannot get worse, so a condition on it could never fail - and a
    condition that cannot fail is the exact defect STP-741 documented.

================================================================
CALIBRATION DEFECT - READ BEFORE WIRING THIS GATE INTO CI
================================================================

The sdk-js-ratchet thresholds above were derived from sdk-js-740, which
is a NARROW scan: 46 files, 6,340 ncloc, 0 vulnerabilities.

The full sdk-js codebase is sdk-js-740-full: 123 files, 16,587 ncloc,
and 36 vulnerabilities. That is 2.7x the files and 2.6x the code, and
the vulnerability count goes from 0 to 36.

So the gate as it stands is calibrated against roughly a third of the
repository. Wired to a full-repo scan it would trip "vulnerabilities
GT 0" on day one and stay red - and a permanently red gate is a gate
somebody switches off, which is worse than no gate.

This is the same failure the narrow scan already produced once as a
REPORT: "all clean" was stated on the strength of 46 files and 0 vulns,
and the full-codebase numbers contradicted it. The instrument measured
a third of the subject and the result was read as covering all of it.

Two things must be settled before this gate goes live, and neither is
mine to settle alone:

  1. SCOPE. What should the gate scan? Candidates:
       - what SHIPS (src/ plus the six plugins), or
       - the whole repository including samples/ and quickstart/.
     The 36 vulnerabilities are concentrated in the half that does not
     ship, which is exactly why the narrow scan looked clean. But the
     samples are the surface the XSS and missing-SRI findings came from
     (fixed in #62), so "does not ship" is not "does not matter".

  2. THRESHOLDS. Whichever scope is chosen, re-derive the numbers
     against THAT scope. Do not carry the sdk-js-ratchet numbers above
     forward - they belong to sdk-js-740 and to nothing else.

CORRECTION 2026-09-14. The line that stood here said sdk-net had no scope
problem - "67 files / 33,294 ncloc is the whole of that repository". That was
FALSE, and it was the same defect as sdk-js's, not an exemption from it.

sdk-net's scan follows StpSDK.sln, and the solution contained THREE projects:
StpSDK, JMSML and the tests. Samples, quickstart and plugins - 12 more
first-party projects - were outside it and therefore invisible to any
solution-based analysis. That is STP-756, fixed in sdk-net #52.

It was not academic. Nine samples did not compile at all, for two independent
reasons found while investigating: an NU1605 package downgrade and a plugin
path casing that cannot resolve off Windows. Nothing noticed, because nothing
built them.

Re-scanned 2026-09-14 with the samples in the solution:

                            before (partial)   after (full scope)
    files                        67                 149
    ncloc                        33,294             50,384
    vulnerabilities              -                  14
    bugs                         -                  28
    code_smells                  846                1,688
    duplicated_lines_density     -                  18.8
    blocker_violations           -                  24
    critical_violations          -                  78
    security_rating              -                  B
    reliability_rating           -                  E
    sqale_rating                 -                  A

sdk-js RE-SCANNED 2026-09-14, main at 9308268 plus the merges of that morning,
same local SonarQube 26.9.0 on :29000:

    files                        126        (partial scan saw 46)
    ncloc                        16,773     (partial scan saw 6,340)
    vulnerabilities              36
    bugs                         48
    code_smells                  633
    duplicated_lines_density     4.0
    blocker_violations           81
    critical_violations          28
    security_rating              B
    reliability_rating           D
    sqale_rating                 A

Those figures reproduce the full-tree numbers this file already predicted
(123 files / 16,587 ncloc / 36 / 81 / 48 / 628 / 4.0 / D / B) to within the
drift of the commits since, which is the corroboration that BOTH measurements
were sound.

Both halves of STP-740 are now derived against the scope that actually ships.
What remains is wiring the gate - and whoever does must assert it EVALUATED its
conditions, not merely that it returned OK. See STP-741.

Recorded on STP-740. The gate was demonstrated to pass AND to fail on
the local container before these objects were deleted; what is
unsettled is the scope it should judge, not whether it functions.

================================================================
CORRECTION 2026-09-14 - the "coverage 0.0" figures above
================================================================

All three scopes above record coverage as 0.0. That number was real but it
was not a measurement of the test suite: it was a measurement of a property
name with a typo in it.

The scan set

    sonar.javascript.lcov.reportsPaths      <- WRONG, note the 's' on 'reports'

and the correct key is

    sonar.javascript.lcov.reportPaths

SonarJS 13.8 registers its coverage sensor behind
`.onlyWhenConfiguration(conf -> conf.hasKey(LCOV_REPORT_PATHS) || ...)`, so an
unrecognised key does not produce a warning, a "file not found", or any other
symptom. The sensor is simply left out of the execution list, and the string
"lcov" never appears in the scanner log at all. A misconfiguration that
reports 0.0% is indistinguishable on a dashboard from an honest 0.0%.

Two things were wrong at once and each hid the other: vitest was also not
emitting an lcov report (its `reporter` list was ['text', 'html']), so even
the correct property would have found nothing. Fixing only one of them would
have produced the same 0.0 and looked like the fix had failed.

Both fixed. Re-measured on the same local SonarQube 26.9.0 on :29000, same
scope as the sdk-js figures above (126 files, 16,773 ncloc):

    coverage          0.0  ->  11.2
    lines_to_cover    6983 ->  7168
    uncovered_lines   6983 ->  6617

with `INFO: Sensor JavaScript/TypeScript Coverage` and `INFO: Analysing
[...coverage/lcov.info]` now present in the log, and no "could not resolve"
warnings - every SF: path in the report matched an indexed file.

11.2% is low because the scope is the whole repository while the suite covers
src/ only: src/ itself measures 94.2% statements, and samples/, quickstart/
and the plugins have no tests at all. That is an honest number for the scope,
and it is the first one this project has had.

None of the seven ratchet conditions is a coverage condition, so no threshold
above needs re-deriving because of this change.

How to check this has not silently regressed again: grep the scanner log for
`Sensor JavaScript/TypeScript Coverage`. If that line is absent, the property
is misspelled or unset - there will be no other sign.

The scan parameters now live in sonar-project.properties at the repository
root rather than in an untracked shell script, so the figures in this file can
be re-derived by someone other than whoever first took them.

================================================================
SUPERSEDED 2026-09-14 - THE RATCHET IN THIS FILE IS NO LONGER THE GATE
================================================================

Read this before using any threshold above. Those numbers are now a historical
measurement, not live guidance, and acting on them would be a mistake.

WHAT REPLACED THEM

SonarQube Cloud automatic analysis is live on this repository and applies the
built-in "Sonar way" quality gate. Its five conditions are all on NEW code:

    new_reliability_rating        <= A
    new_security_rating           <= A
    new_maintainability_rating    <= A
    new_duplicated_lines_density  <= 3%
    new_security_hotspots_reviewed = 100%

That is strictly better than the absolute-count ratchet this file describes,
and for a reason worth stating: a new-code gate does not require the existing
debt to be paid before it becomes useful. The ratchet had to be re-derived
every time the codebase moved; this does not. The ~600 pre-existing findings
gate nothing, and the next regression still goes red.

The gate is confirmed to EVALUATE its conditions - all five come back with
actual values, not the empty `conditions: []` that made the engine's gate
incapable of failing for sixty runs (STP-741). Check that property, not just
the OK.

WHY THE NUMBERS ABOVE MUST NOT BE USED AS THRESHOLDS

They came from a LOCAL SonarQube Community Build container. Measured the same
day against Cloud, the same code produces materially different numbers:

    sdk-js     local 617 issues     Cloud 646
    sdk-net    local 1,580 issues   Cloud 840

Not drift - a 2x divergence on sdk-net, and in both directions by category
(Cloud reports 17 bugs where local reports 6; local reports 1,560 smells where
Cloud reports 806). Two causes, both understood:

  - Community Build is deliberately rule-reduced. It drops the advanced .NET
    dataflow rules and advanced SAST that Cloud runs, so Cloud finds real
    defects local cannot see.
  - Correct test classification (sonar.tests) moves hundreds of findings out
    of the main measurement.

A local scanner is a PRE-FLIGHT, not a gate. Use it to answer presence and
absence in minutes - "did my suppression actually fire?" - and never to set a
threshold. Threshold numbers come from the analysis that actually gates.

WHERE CONFIGURATION LIVES NOW

    .sonarcloud.properties     read by Cloud AUTOMATIC ANALYSIS. This is the
                               one that affects the gate.
    sonar-project.properties   IGNORED by automatic analysis. Still correct for
                               local scans and any future CI-based analysis,
                               which is why it remains.

Automatic analysis cannot import coverage at all, so the lcov wiring described
earlier in this file produces no Cloud coverage figure. That is a known and
accepted cost of this analysis method, not a defect - the numbers are still
produced and uploaded as CI artifacts.

Everything above this section is kept because the measurements were real and
the reasoning about scope still holds. It is history, not instruction.
